blocks.text: Good morning Barbara,

To close out the reconciliation question below: the status history now ties to the year-end census for every year of the study period except the first. We can begin the termination and retirement tabulations on the years that tie, and add the first year once one coding question is settled.
For your staff's reference, the reconciliation ran as follows.
1. We took each year-end census and rolled its active count forward to the next year-end, using the status changes recorded in the history file.
2. For every year after the first, the rolled-forward count agrees with the following census once the rehires flagged in the file are counted back in as actives.

3. In the first year, a group of records leaves the active census with no status change recorded. Most of the same people reappear that year under a new employee number, which points to internal transfers rather than terminations. The file itself does not say so.

Could someone in your benefits area confirm whether those records are transfers and, if they are, send the old and new employee number for each person? Until we have that, we will hold them out of the first-year termination counts instead of treating them as withdrawals, and the {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}} data summary will describe that treatment. Any first-year rate we show before then is preliminary.
Best
Experience Study Working Session: Minutes
Experience study for {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}. Working session held by conference call, with the first tabulations circulated to attendees the day before.

We met to settle the data the study relies on and to take a first look at the plan's experience. Recommended assumptions were not on the agenda. They follow once the tabulations are final, and nothing recorded here should be read as one. The study is being performed under ASOP No. 35, which governs the selection of demographic assumptions.
Attendees
Data relied on

We started with the data, since every rate in the study rests on it. David Sherman reported that the status history now ties to the year-end census in every year of the study period. The last open item had been the group of first-year records that left the active census with no recorded change of status. Barbara Hall confirmed that they were internal transfers, which the payroll system had entered as new hires under new employee numbers. Her staff sent the old and new numbers, Megan Dudley linked them, and David reran the reconciliation. It holds.

Megan raised a smaller point. A few retiree records have no date of birth. Barbara expects the benefits office can supply the dates from the original retirement applications. Megan set out what we will do if it cannot. Those records will be left out of the mortality tabulation. They will not be given an assumed age, and the study will say how many were left out.
First look at the experience

Jeffrey Ochoa took us through the tabulations. Each one compares the terminations, retirements or deaths the plan actually recorded with the number the current assumptions would have predicted. He kept the observed results apart from anything we might later recommend, and these minutes keep the same line.

On terminations, the data show more departures than expected in the first years of service and fewer than expected after that. On retirements, the counts run below expected in the early retirement window and close to expected at older ages. On mortality, the plan recorded fewer retiree deaths than the current table predicts.

Barbara asked whether the early-service result might come from a single unusual hiring year and not from a lasting pattern. It might. Jeffrey will split those results by year of hire before we draw anything from them.

Our view at this stage is limited. The plan's own experience is not large enough to set every rate by itself, and the mortality result rests on few deaths. Where the data are thin we will weight them against a published table, as ASOP No. 25 provides. The report will show the weight given, so that it can be checked.
Agreed actions
The draft recommendations depend on each of these items. We have listed them in the order they need to be done.

blocks.text: Our thanks to Barbara and her staff for turning the transfer question around so quickly. We would ask for any corrections to these minutes before the draft recommendations go out, so that the minutes and the recommendations rest on the same account of the data.
Experience Study: Status at the Midpoint

For {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}. Prepared by David Sherman, Senior Analyst. The study is at its midpoint. This report sets out the work done so far and what remains, and it makes no recommendation on any assumption.
In Brief

The data work for terminations, retirements and mortality is finished. The status history reconciles to the census in every year of the study period, and the experience for each of the three has been tabulated against the current assumptions. No assumption has yet been recommended. The study is on schedule and within budget.

One piece of data is still outstanding. The salary increase analysis needs the pay history for the earliest years of the study period, which we requested in the data summary. That analysis cannot start until the history arrives, and it is the item most likely to affect the schedule.
Work Completed This Period

1. We reconciled the status history to the year-end census for every year of the study period. The last gap, a group of internal transfers that payroll had recorded as new hires, closed when Megan Dudley linked the old and new employee numbers your staff supplied.

2. We received dates of birth for all but a few of the retiree records that lacked them. As agreed at the working session, the remaining records are excluded from the mortality tabulation, and the data summary lists each one.
3. We issued the data summary. It records every change made to the files, the source of each change, and every record excluded.

4. Jeffrey Ochoa split the early-service termination results by year of hire. The higher rate of departure appears in each hiring year, not in one, so it does not look like the effect of a single unusual year.
5. Robert Lawrence reviewed the tabulations and the approach to credibility. Drafting of the recommendations can begin.
Observed Experience

The table compares the experience the plan recorded with what the current assumptions predicted. These are measurements. None of them is a recommendation, and none should be read as a decision to change a rate.

blocks.text: What We Have Assumed

We have relied on the census, the status history and the benefit records as your staff provided them. We reviewed them for consistency and completeness, as ASOP No. 23 requires, but we have not audited them.

Three treatments in the tabulations are our choices, not facts in the data, and the report will state each of them. Transferred employees are carried as continuing service. Rehired employees re-enter the active group from the date of rehire. Retiree records without a date of birth are left out instead of being given an assumed age.
Budget

Time charged through the midpoint is consistent with the fee of {{fact:f:E-2019-001.fee}} set out in the engagement letter, and we do not expect the remaining work to exceed it. If the pay history needs a second request or substantial correction, the added work could affect that expectation. We will raise it with you before that work begins.
Work Remaining
1. The salary increase analysis, once the pay history for the earliest years arrives. David Sherman will lead it.

2. Draft recommended assumptions for termination, retirement and mortality. Jeffrey Ochoa will prepare them, with the basis for each and the weight given to the plan's own experience. The mortality recommendation will also address future improvement, measured against the MP-2018 scale the Society of Actuaries published last October.
3. A working session with your staff to go through the draft recommendations before the report is written.
4. The draft report, followed by the final report once your comments are addressed. Robert Lawrence will sign the final report.
